questions.question: Which mechanism best explains typical GERD?
choices: Lower esophageal barrier weakness or inappropriate relaxation allows gastric reflux
Complete absence of gastric acid
Pulmonary artery obstruction
Colonic transmural inflammation
questions.explanation: GERD results when the lower esophageal sphincter/diaphragm barrier is weak or relaxes inappropriately, allowing gastric contents to reflux into the esophagus.

questions.question: What are the two most common causes of peptic ulcer disease?
choices: H. pylori infection and NSAID exposure
Asthma and COPD
AF and heart failure
Iron deficiency and B12 deficiency
questions.explanation: H. pylori infection and NSAID exposure are the two common causes of peptic ulcer disease. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection.

questions.question: A patient has melena, tachycardia, dizziness, and near-syncope. What is the priority FNP decision?
choices: Schedule routine reflux follow-up
Recognize possible significant GI bleeding and arrange emergency evaluation
Treat only iron deficiency
Assume the stool color is dietary
questions.explanation: Melena with tachycardia, dizziness, or near-syncope can indicate significant GI bleeding and reduced perfusion. Emergency evaluation is required.

questions.question: Which finding is most consistent with an inflammatory/structural bowel disorder rather than typical IBS?
choices: Recurrent pain related to defecation with no alarm features
Nocturnal bloody diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia
Symptoms that vary with stress only
Normal bowel habits
questions.explanation: GI bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, anemia, fever, and inflammatory findings are alarm features that need evaluation for IBD, infection, malignancy, or other structural disease.

questions.question: Which description best fits ulcerative colitis?
choices: Patchy transmural inflammation anywhere from mouth to anus
Continuous colonic mucosal inflammation beginning at the rectum
A functional disorder without inflammation
Acute obstruction of the pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: UC typically causes continuous mucosal inflammation in the colon beginning at the rectum, whereas Crohn disease may be patchy, transmural, and involve any GI segment.

questions.question: A patient has weeks of urgent bloody diarrhea, fatigue, weight loss, and nocturnal symptoms. What is the best general approach?
choices: Diagnose IBS without testing
Consider IBD and infection, assess severity and arrange appropriate evaluation
Reassure because young adults do not get inflammatory disease
Treat only the abdominal pain
questions.explanation: Bloody diarrhea, weight loss, urgency, fatigue, and nocturnal symptoms are concerning for inflammatory or infectious disease, not routine IBS. Evaluate severity, hydration, anemia, and need for referral/escalation.

questions.question: Why can a patient with upper GI bleeding have a hemoglobin that does not initially reflect total blood loss?
choices: Hemoglobin is unrelated to bleeding
Equilibration after acute blood loss may take time, so hemodynamics and ongoing bleeding matter
Upper GI bleeding always increases hemoglobin
Only chronic bleeding changes hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Early hemoglobin may not fully reflect acute blood loss before equilibration. Vital signs, perfusion, symptoms, and evidence of ongoing bleeding are essential.

questions.question: Which patient with “indigestion” needs a high level of concern for ACS rather than automatic GERD labeling?
choices: A patient with exertional pressure, dyspnea, nausea, diabetes, and hypertension
A patient with a stable history of occasional post-meal heartburn only
A patient with no symptoms
A patient with isolated seasonal allergies
questions.explanation: Exertional pressure/discomfort with dyspnea, nausea, and cardiovascular risk factors can represent ACS even when described as indigestion. Emergency cardiovascular evaluation is appropriate.

questions.question: Which is an alarm feature that should prompt evaluation for colorectal or other structural disease when clinically appropriate?
choices: Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia or persistent blood in stool
A single day of mild gas after a large meal
No change in bowel habits
Symptom improvement with hydration
questions.explanation: Persistent blood in stool, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, persistent bowel change, or abdominal pain can indicate structural disease and warrant appropriate evaluation.

questions.question: A patient has sudden severe persistent abdominal pain with guarding and a rigid abdomen. What is the appropriate disposition?
choices: Routine outpatient IBS evaluation
Emergency assessment for a possible surgical/perforation process
Wait one month for symptom tracking
Treat only with dietary advice
questions.explanation: Peritoneal signs, rigid abdomen, and severe persistent pain are emergency red flags. They may reflect perforation or another acute surgical process and require immediate evaluation.
